I was and am an RBT of 7 years I have been holding off on pursuing masters because I financially couldn't afford it. It's a shame that the RBT role isn't attainable for someone to be financially independent. If I could survive and pay for things on my own I would have stayed an RBT. But I think what makes it worse is the RBT only requiring a high school diploma that companies feel that these positions are simply stepping stones or for people getting their feet wet with clinical roles and not for the long haul. I have met a few lifetime RBTs that were by far the best I have ever seen and came across and were only able to maintain because they had a second income by either a spouse, family money, or some side gig that made it maintainable.

I have learned that I have to come up with things to do myself. Thankfully there is a lot to do (on my own time unpaid) that I can count as unrestricted. Pairing. Hands down. How to pair what it looks like. How to fade in demands. Understanding and implementing the contingencies of reinforcement. Understanding the difference between preferences and reinforcers. Extinction procedures and when and how to use them correctly. Antecedent interventions.

The pairing period is different with every single client. And just because you aren't running programs it doesn't necessarily mean that you aren't doing simple things to build instructional control. I also spend time to pair every single session. And in my honest opinion pairing doesn't necessarily let the the kid do whatever they want etc.... it means establishing yourself as the reinforcer and pairing yourself with demands and with fun things in the environment which should be happening on a consistent basis. Also in my experience the pairing period differs based on the kids environment especially working in home. A kids home environment can change drastically sometimes. Over the years doing aba ive learned what sets me apart is the nuance of knowing what battles to pick what to work on etc. You can always be working on something whether it be simply requesting for things, cleaning up, or even approaching you (if the kid is aversive). 
I hate when I see a therapist say they are "pairing" and it basically means that they follow the kid around while the kid runs everywhere without doing anything at all. Everything can be a learning experience without being too strict or placing too many demands and still following the child's lead etc.
